name: Elena Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and lead a carpentry crew putting timber hoardings and temporary gates around the station extension. I have a vocational trade certificate. I set out braces and inspect fixings before the public route opens. I like making a safe path through a messy site; delivery lists that miss a slope are the nuisance.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is work and home life like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My lead rate is high, and similar building work is plentiful nearby. My partner works at the municipal garage, our children are grown, and we have almost a year's household expenses saved. I'd like to finish paid site work at 66 if our income allows. I never use AI myself; the office can make lists, but I check the actual timber and anchors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our timber crew the software can tidy a delivery list, but it cannot tell whether a rail-side hoarding is anchored into solid ground. Let the builders inspect the fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead carpenter wage is good, and we have nearly a year's household expenses set aside. My partner still works at the municipal garage, and our children are grown. If work stays familiar, I can aim to finish paid site work at 66, provided our income plan still adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the hoarding installation at the station extension and checking every anchor before we sign it off. I won't start using AI for my own work just because an office clerk sends a neater list. I'll continue the usual monthly savings from my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A small office saving does not change my paid site hours, and the reserve gives us time to make decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the delivery list miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last delivery list omitted the brace needed beside the temporary pedestrian gate. I marked it on the site drawing and made sure it arrived before the gate was opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How firm is your retirement age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 I would look at our actual income and the cost of living before stopping. Our household reserve is a cushion, not an automatic retirement cheque.

say: **Timber lists** can improve without replacing a fixing inspection.
The **site crew** must check ground anchors before opening a pedestrian route.
think: My **lead wage** remains secure in this mild outcome.
Nearly a year of **expenses saved** supports a conditional plan to stop at 66.
do: **Lead** the station hoarding installation and inspect each ground anchor.
**Continue** regular monthly saving from the higher site wage.
feel: **Calm** because paid site work continues and savings are substantial.
S0.quote: Our household reserve is a cushion, not an automatic retirement cheque.
fieldNote: Elena is **resistant to AI** in her own practice, though she accepts a useful office list.
A **strong reserve** and high site wage support a possible age-66 exit, which depends on income then.

steps.text: Keep leading hoarding installation and inspecting each anchor
Continue monthly saving from current site wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site steward to insist on paid instruction for anyone handed a new drawing system. If planners cut their own hours, the work still needs a carpenter to check the gate and brace on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The faster office schedule might push more sections onto our crew. I expect my own wage to hold for now because the physical hoarding work remains, but I'd dislike being rushed into signing a fixing I had not tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask our union steward to put drawing review time and a named human sign-off into the next site meeting. I'll keep checking the actual anchors with the crew and record any mismatched AI lists. I won't take up a new AI tool unless there is evidence it improves safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the rush and who carries the liability. I am not forecasting a cut in my own paid hours in this slower change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the contractor to provide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the contractor to leave enough paid time for two people to inspect a section before pedestrians pass it. That is a safety demand we can raise together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if an AI drawing changes overnight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the supplier changes the drawing without marking the revision, I'll stop that section and have the site engineer identify the load path. A fast list is not permission to open an unsafe gate.

say: The **union steward** should secure paid checking time and human sign-off.
A **revised drawing** does not authorize an untested pedestrian gate.
think: My **paid site hours** look intact while physical hoardings still require crews.
A rushed **inspection schedule** could make safe sign-off harder.
do: **Raise** paid drawing review and human sign-off with the union steward.
**Record** mismatches and inspect the ground anchors with the crew.
feel: **Uneasy** about rushed inspections, while her own wage remains secure.
S1.quote: A fast list is not permission to open an unsafe gate.
fieldNote: Her **collective demand** concerns paid safety checks, not a personal request for training.
She remains **resistant to AI** and expects site carpentry hours to remain for now.

steps.text: Raise paid review and human sign-off through union steward
Keep recording mismatches and inspecting site anchors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 could plan our temporary works, and capable robots around 2031 could put up some hoardings. I'd tell the crew not to accept a shorter roster without a safe plan for the gates and a wage plan for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when those robots reach physical site work, three years before I hope to leave at 66. Even with almost a year of expenses saved, a substantial cut to my higher wage could change whether we can stop then. There are other builders nearby, but I would need a real job that pays enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union steward for the contractor's proposed crew numbers and push for paid supervised inspection training if an actual place is offered and the qualification is recognized locally. If my roster is cut, I'll apply to posted local site-inspector jobs only where my certificate qualifies me and the stated pay and safe hours cover our costs. I'll keep the present carpentry wage while those conditions are checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the wage close to retirement, though I have some room to act. I would rather qualify for a real inspection post than pretend a robot needs no checker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would inspection training have to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the trainer to show us how to load-test a gate fixing and stop the machine safely. An unpaid demonstration on an empty site is not a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid course is unavailable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no paid course place appears, I'll stay with the hoarding crew as long as the wage holds and apply for posted local carpentry work when hours are cut. The alternative must pay enough to keep our age-66 plan credible.

say: **2028 thinking AI** may plan temporary works before robots build hoardings around 2031.
The union should demand **crew numbers**, safe checks and paid training places.
think: At **63**, a cut to my higher wage could delay a hoped-for age-66 exit.
Strong **savings** and plentiful local builders give options, subject to real pay.
do: **Seek** actual paid, recognized inspection training with supervised safety practice.
**Apply** for posted local inspection roles after qualifying if roster and pay justify moving.
**Apply** for posted local carpentry work if no course and hours are cut.
feel: **Anxious** about a late wage cut despite a strong reserve.
S2.quote: An unpaid demonstration on an empty site is not a job offer.
fieldNote: At robot arrival she is **63**, so a pay cut can disrupt the conditional age-66 exit.
She separates **training** from an eventual qualifying application and from the no-course carpentry fallback.

steps.text: Ask union steward for crew numbers and paid training places
Attend recognized inspection training if offered paid supervised place
Apply for posted local inspection job if qualified, roster cut, safe, pay sufficient
Apply for posted local carpentry job if no paid course, hours cut, pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI matures around 2031 and site robots arrive around 2034, I would tell the crew to use those five years for real safety rules. A robot setting a hoarding still needs somebody accountable for the public side of the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when capable robots arrive, the age I hope to stop paid work. Our savings are strong, but I cannot promise retirement before seeing our actual income then. If we need another paid year, a smaller site roster could still hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll bring proposed robot gate checks to the union safety committee and ask our contractor for a paid practical inspection place if it develops the machines. If the place is offered with wages, supervised practice and a recognized certificate, I'll attend. If I am still working at 66 and site hours are cut, I'll apply for posted local inspection roles after qualifying only if the pay and safe duties meet our income need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy because there is time to plan, yet the machine date sits right on my hoped-for retirement year. I won't count an unoffered course or a future vacancy as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the practical test involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practical test should include an uneven base and a gate used by pedestrians, with the area closed until a qualified person checks the load. I would not practice that on a live public route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your income allows retirement at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our income at 66 lets me stop, I'll retire then and won't pursue the inspection role. If it does not, the posted salary and actual safe hours decide whether I move from the carpentry crew.

The **safety committee** should require a qualified human check at public gates.
think: I reach **66** around robot arrival, when my hoped-for exit depends on actual income.
A **smaller roster** matters only if I still need paid work then.
do: **Retire** at original age-sixty-six target only if household income covers living costs.
**Attend** paid recognized inspection training if a supervised place is offered.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work if still employed, qualified and hours cut.
feel: **Uneasy** about the timing of robots and conditional retirement.
S3.quote: I won't count an unoffered course or a future vacancy as income.
fieldNote: The **age-66 exit** is conditional on household income, not a guaranteed pension.
Her **training and application** occur only if offered and necessary; retirement ends the employment path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI reaches sites in 2036 and capable robots build hoardings around 2039, I'd tell the crew that rules still need to be written before any machine works beside pedestrians. We can test methods without pretending every site is flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and about 71 when robots do physical site work. I hope to finish paid work at 66 if our income allows, so I may already be out of the trade. If that plan slips, the strong reserve helps, but a high wage is still hard to replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep earning and adding to our monthly savings while we review the age-66 income plan each year. I'll press the union safety committee for public-gate robot standards, whether or not I am still on a site in 2039. If I need to work beyond 66 and our contractor cuts hours, I'll apply for posted local carpentry or inspection work that I actually qualify for, with safe duties and enough stated pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about what later crews may face, though the long runway and savings give me room. My own exposure depends on whether I still need a site wage after 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pass on to younger carpenters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would give the younger crew our anchor-check sheets and explain why the gate next to the sloping curb needed an extra brace. It is a practical record, not a promise that the same machine will work there later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will you decide whether to stop at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At each annual review we'll compare expected living costs with actual household income. At sixty-six I leave paid work only if household income covers living costs; otherwise I keep earning and check local vacancies.

**Public-gate standards** need worker input before site machines operate beside pedestrians.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture troubles you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 change troubles me most. At 63, a shorter roster could interrupt the high wage we need to make a 66 exit work. Paid recognized inspection training, a real posted job at sufficient pay and a crew safety plan would give me choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: What should I have asked that I did not?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs for the gate after a robot fixes it beside the public path. The pedestrian route cannot be opened on an untested anchor.

headlineQuote: The pedestrian route cannot be opened on an untested anchor.
portrait: **Elena**, 58, is a lead site carpenter with a vocational trade certificate and a high wage.
Her **strong reserve** covers almost a year of expenses; her partner works and their children are grown.
She **never uses AI** herself and insists on physical inspection of hoarding anchors and pedestrian gates.
She hopes to stop at **66** if income permits, and seeks paid safety training if robots threaten her roster.
biggestWorry: **Fast site robots** around 2031 could shorten her high-paid roster at 63, delaying a conditional age-66 exit.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid recognized inspection place**, clear crew plan and real local role with sufficient pay would give her choices.
